catalog_quote: 2.11 Accent There is typically one accent per lexical item, realised as high tone . However, it is not clear whether accent here is best described as pitch - accent or stress - accent . In many words, the accent induces vowel centralisation in syllables around it, suggesting stress . On the other hand, certain words have tone - like features as, e.g., in palê ngá ' how many . ' For the most part, accent is predictable . Prominence is marked with an acute accent (') . 2.11.1 Accent in nouns With di- and trisyllabic stems, the accent typically falls on the first syllable of the stem . (12) li - hí.mba (cl.5) chi - dú.li (cl.7) ... There are exceptions to this generalisation . In classes 1, 3 and 14, the accent falls on the noun class prefix . In class 7, it also appears on the class prefix, just in those cases where the stem begins with labial / w / or / mb / . (13) mú - ha.vi (cl.1) mú - ha.nga (cl.3) chí - mbo.ndi (cl.7) ... Trisyllabic stems having a final NCV syllable realise the accent on the penultimate syllable . (14) n - ko.ló.ngo (cl.1) ... Disyllabic reduplicated stems realise the accent on the noun class prefix: CV - CVCV . CVCV RED (17) lí - ka.tu.ka.tu ... 2.11.2 Accent in verbs ... As with most nouns, accent on verbs typically falls on the first syllable of the stem (demarcated by -), whether the verb occurs in infinitival form or is conjugated . The sole exceptions arise with the imperfective -aa and modal suffixes -ayi and -aa, which shift the accent to the penultimate mora, hence STEM - á.a .

new_statements.rule_in_words: One culminative accent per word, phonetically a high tone (author leaves open whether it is a pitch accent or a stress accent, noting vowel centralisation in neighbouring syllables). Its position is morphologically determined: the first syllable of the stem in both nouns and verbs, regardless of prefixes or inflection; hence not penultimate (unlike neighbouring Tanzanian Ngoni/Matengo).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in the visible text ('one accent per lexical item').
new_statements.exceptions: Nouns: in some nouns the accent falls on the noun-class prefix (mu'-ha.vi cl.1, mu'-ha.nga cl.3), and in class 7 on chi'- only when the stem begins with /w/ or /mb/ (chi'-mbo.ndi); trisyllabic stems with a final NCV syllable take the accent on the penultimate syllable (n-ko.lo'.ngo cl.1); monosyllabic reduplicated stems accent the initial stem syllable (li'-ka.tu.ka.tu as printed in snippet). Verbs: imperfective -aa and modal suffixes -ayi / -aa shift the accent to the penultimate mora (STEM-a'.a). Some words show tone-like behaviour (pale^ nga' 'how many').
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word (citation forms of nouns, infinitives and conjugated verbs); accent marked with acute in the chapter's transcription. Phrase-level behaviour not visible in the snippets. Text was accessed only as overlapping Google Books snippet windows that chain into continuous prose; not checked against the printed page.
new_statements.identity_note: Botne (2019) describes the Tanzanian variety of Chimpoto (Mbinga district, eastern shore of Lake Nyasa; consultant M. P. Mwingira); his introduction notes dialect differences between Malawian and Tanzanian varieties and within the Tanzanian variety. Same languoid as mpot1240 (ISO mpa); no separate glottocode for the dialects.
